job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Ben Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Great to meet you. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing a master's in robotics, so I'm usually in the lab soldering a gripper onto an arm or arguing with my code. I live in student housing in Halden with five people and one fridge. Three evenings a week I tutor first-year students in programming for cash, and weekends I work on a drone idea with my friend Luca. I use AI tools all day, for code, for reading papers and for writing emails I don't want to write.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say okay, good, we can stop panicking and build useful things. I'd tell my coursemates the tools are helpful but not magic, and that the interesting work is still in making machines do things in the real world. Then I'd go back to the lab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for robotics but I'm still stretched. I've got a big loan, about ten days of living costs saved, and not many robotics jobs close to Halden. There's one warehouse firm, Corvane Systems, where I interned, and the rest are two trains away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, finish a working demo of the drone project and apply to Corvane and about thirty other robotics firms. I'd also keep the tutoring going. I'd also enter a student robotics competition in spring, because a good result gets you noticed more than a CV.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty optimistic, actually. A bit jittery about money, but I like having a world I understand. I'd probably celebrate with a pizza and then check my bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a plateau change what you and Luca are building?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's tiny. Luca and I put in about forty pounds a month each for parts. The drone does inspection of roofs, and a local roofer, Mr Hale, said he'd try it for free. That's the whole pipeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the money situation like for the drone project?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I use the tools already, so it would just be the same tools and maybe slower progress. The part that would change is hiring: if the tools don't take junior jobs, firms keep hiring graduates the usual way, which suits me.

say: I'd say the tools are **helpful but not magic**, and the interesting work is still making machines act in the real world.
think: Plateau is good for robotics, but I'm **stretched**: a big loan and ten days of living costs.
Few robotics jobs are close, so I'd need **Corvane** or a move.

Apply to **Corvane and about 30** other robotics firms.
Enter a **student robotics competition** in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly the moment to learn how to build with the tools, not just use them. I'd tell people to try things in public, post a project every month and get used to change. I'd also say we should make sure the training is free, because I'd have had no hope without a scholarship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fairly hopeful. Software tasks get cheap, but somebody has to make the machines that touch the world, and that's my field. The pure-software juniors get hit, but robotics and mechatronics need a person who can do code and hardware.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pitch the drone idea to a couple of roofing firms, set up a small paid pilot and apply for a graduate job as backup. I'd use AI tools for the code and spend the time I save on testing in the field. And I'd start a small newsletter on building with the tools, because teaching helps my own learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit of imposter nerves, too. I'd feel like I'm on a fast bike on a good road, but there's gravel on the corner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots spread slowly in this one. Does that help or hurt the drone idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slower robots help the drone idea, because there's time to build it before everyone does. It hurts a little, because if hands-on work is safer for a while, more people will try it, and competition goes up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell first-years who ask you if coding is worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes, but learn to build things, not just to write code. Pure coding is the first thing that gets cheap. I'd tell them to put a motor on something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's get serious now, with a public fund for people who lose work and a limit on how fast firms can swap in AI. I wouldn't be the loudest, but I'd put my name on a letter. And I'd tell my friends to build something with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm worried but I'd move fast. By 2028 the thinking work is done by AI, and a master's in robotics is partly thinking work. The hands-on side of what I do, like the wiring and the testing, lasts to 2031, and I'd bet on that gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the thesis polish and get the drone service working for money, even for a few pounds a roof. I'd also apply to Corvane and similar firms for a technician role instead of an engineer role, which is a step down but a step in. And I'd ask Luca to quit his course so we do it full time, which is a big ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with energy. It's like standing at the start of a race you didn't enter. I'd want to run rather than watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is short. How does the drone project change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hardware gets built by people for three more years, and that's my window. After that robots build robots, and I'd need to own the machines, not just fix them. So the plan is to own a small fleet of drones by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the robot delay of three years mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might not make any money. The drone idea could fail in two weeks. If it does, I'd go for the technician route, which pays, and keep the idea as a hobby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to do it properly: retraining, a safety net and rules on how firms use it. I'd write that in a student paper and post it. I'd also say people should try the tools now, not wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm pretty calm about myself. I'd have a job by next year, and by 2031 a few years of robotics experience, which is the thing the machines will need people for. I'd still have the loan, but I'd be earning against it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a graduate robotics job at a firm like Corvane and run the drone project on the side. I'd use the tools to do my day job faster, then spend the time learning how to make machines safer. I'd also put twenty percent of each pay cheque into an index fund, to have a stake in the thing replacing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good. There's some dread on the horizon but it's not near. I'd go to the pub more, which Luca would say is a bad sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years. Does that change the drone idea, or the job plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay it down aggressively for two years, then put what's left into a fund and some parts for the drone. The loan is a number I can beat. The other things, the machines and the roof firms, are bets, and I'd keep them small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. The job pays the bills, and the drone gives me a way out if the job stops. I'd think of it as a two-legged stool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the decade is a gift and we should use it to build things that matter, like better care robots and cleaner infrastructure. I'd tell people not to waste it on panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm optimistic. I'd have ten years of building, probably a small company or a senior role. The change is coming, but I'd be on the right side of it, because I make machines, not just prompts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work for a few years at a robotics firm and learn how real factories run. Then I'd start a company, maybe with Luca, building inspection robots for buildings and bridges. I'd keep the loan to a payment I don't notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Even a bit giddy. I'd be careful not to get overconfident, because I've seen firms fall hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With a decade, what does your career look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in about three years. I'd want the first couple to learn how a business runs and to save a cushion. Then I'd go on my own, when the debts are small and the AI tools do the admin I hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to start your own thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A normal middle-class life, I suppose. A flat, a partner, maybe a dog. And a company that has a few people on payroll who would otherwise have nothing to do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it lands before I've built anything. What would help is a start-up grant for graduates who lose jobs and access to cheap parts. Even a small fund would do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about luck. I've been lucky: a lab with equipment, a friend who thinks like me and a scholarship. Not everyone has those, so I'd say luck is the thing nobody talks about when they say adapt.

headlineQuote: I'd say luck is the thing nobody talks about when they say adapt.
portrait: Ben is a **24-year-old** top mechatronics graduate doing a master's in robotics, living in a shared student house in Halden.
He uses AI tools **all day** and tutors first-years while building a roof-inspection drone with his friend Luca.
He's centre in politics, **adaptive** and optimistic, though debt and few local jobs keep him stretched.
His mood runs from **uneasy** to anxious and only the two-year world truly worries him.
He bets on hardware and owning machines, and thinks luck is what no one mentions.
biggestWorry: The **two-year scenario**, because it comes before he has built anything of his own.
whatWouldHelp: A **start-up grant** for graduates who lose jobs and access to cheap parts.
